content: Tinea versicolor, also known as pityriasis versicolor, is a common superficial fungal infection of the skin caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur (previously referred to as Pityrosporum ovale). This yeast is a normal component of the human skin microbiota but can become pathogenic under certain conditions, such as in warm and humid environments. Symptoms The clinical presentation of tinea versicolor includes the following features: The appearance of oval or irregularly shaped macules or patches, typically measuring between 1/4 to 1 inch in diameter. These lesions often coalesce to form larger areas of involvement. Fine scaling of the affected skin, which may produce a superficial, ash-like scale. Lesions may vary in color, appearing pale, dark tan, or pink, often with a reddish undertone. The pigmentation can darken when the patient is overheated, such as after a hot shower or physical exercise. The borders of the lesions are usually well-defined. The most commonly affected areas include the back, underarms, upper arms, chest, lower legs, and neck. Occasionally, the face may also be involved. Microscopic examination of the lesions often reveals the characteristic spaghetti and meatball appearance, which refers to the combination of round yeast cells and short hyphal filaments. In individuals with darker skin tones, hypopigmentation (loss of skin color) is frequently observed, whereas those with lighter skin tones may exhibit hyperpigmentation (increased skin color). These pigmentary changes have led to the colloquial term sun fungus for this condition. Diagnosis Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the characteristic appearance of the lesions. Confirmation can be achieved through microscopic examination of skin scrapings using potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation, which reveals the typical fungal morphology. Differential Diagnosis Tinea versicolor must be distinguished from other dermatological conditions that present with erythematous, scaly, annular, and pruritic rashes. Differential diagnoses include: Tinea corporis (ringworm) Seborrheic dermatitis Pityriasis rosea Vitiligo Erythrasma Prevalence Tinea versicolor is a common condition, affecting an estimated 2–8% of the population in the United States. It is more prevalent among adolescents and young adults, particularly in warm and humid climates. The yeast thrives on skin lipids and dead skin cells, which contribute to its proliferation. Treatment Management of tinea versicolor involves the use of topical or systemic antifungal agents. Recommended treatments include: Topical therapies: 5% selenium sulfide (e.g., Selsun® shampoo in the UK, though not Selsun Blue, which contains only 1%) or 2% ketoconazole (e.g., Nizoral® ointment or shampoo). These are applied to dry skin and washed off after 10 minutes, repeated daily for 2 weeks. Other topical antifungal agents, such as clotrimazole, miconazole, or terbinafine, may also be used but are less commonly recommended. Hydrogen peroxide has been reported to reduce symptoms and, in some cases, resolve the condition. Oral antifungal medications (prescription-only): A single dose of 400 mg ketoconazole or fluconazole. Ketoconazole 200 mg daily for 7 days. Itraconazole 400 mg daily for 3–7 days. Single-dose regimens can be enhanced by inducing sweating 1–2 hours after administration (e.g., through exercise). Patients are advised to allow the sweat to evaporate and delay showering for 24 hours, leaving a film of the medication on the skin. Recurrence and Prevention Recurrence of tinea versicolor is common. Preventative measures include: Intermittent application of topical antifungal agents, such as tea tree oil. Adding a small amount of anti-dandruff shampoo to bathwater to reduce fungal colonization. By adhering to these treatment and prevention strategies, the condition can be effectively managed, though long-term maintenance may be necessary to prevent recurrence.
